newsitem.title: USA: U.S. still open to mission in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. still open to mission in Zaire.

text.p: The United States is open to joining an international force to help refugees in central Africa if it has a clear mission, a senior State Department official said Wednesday.

"We remain open-minded to a multinational force operation with a clearly defined mission," Richard Bogosian, the department's coordinator for Rwanda and Burundi said at a House of Representatives hearing.
"On the other hand, we do not want to commit to an operation without knowing, for example, the whereabouts of the target population, just for the sake of 'doing something'," he said.

President Bill Clinton said several weeks ago that the United States would be willing to send some 4,000 troops as part of a multinational force in eastern Zaire to help get food and supplies to an estimated 1.1 million refugees fleeing the border into the Zairean interior.
But many of those refugees -- Washington has said 600,000 -- have since returned to Rwanda, throwing plans for the international force into disarray.

Phyllis Oakley, the assistant secretary of State for Refugees, said it was believed between 200,000 and 400,000 refugees from the Zairian camps were unaccounted for, though reliable numbers were hard to obtain.

"At this point, we simply do not know how many dispersed refugees and displaced Zairians there are or in what condition they may be," she told members of the House International Relations Committee. "It is obviously critical that the international community have ground access in order to assess numbers and needs."
She said there were also over 700,000 refugees in Tanzania from Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire.
Canada, which has offered to lead a multinational mission in central Africa, hosted a planning meeting in Ottawa last Friday but no decisions were made.

Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Vincent Kern said 446 U.S. military personnel were in the area including 328 in Entebbe, 22 in Kigali and 96 in Mombasa. He said the Pentagon was making plans for airdrops of food and humanitarian supplies if that became necessary.
Bogosian said Washington would back an international conference to resolve the conflicts in central Africa.

Representative Donald Payne, D-New Jersey, the chairman of the Congressional Black Caucus, urged the administration to stop stalling and take action. "We cannot afford to stand by and let thousands of people die while we make up our minds," he said.
Representative Chris Smith, R-New Jersey, who chaired the hearing, said steps should be taken to resettle or protect Rwandans who do not want to return home because they fear persecution.
